items.title: Venezuela’s People Problem
items.description: D ays after two deadly earthquakes struck northern Venezuela on June 24, killing at least 6,000 people and injuring tens of thousands more, the Venezuelan Seismological Research Foundation, known as Funvisis, made an unusual public plea : Could whoever had taken one of its GPS sensors please give it back? For 13 years, the high-precision instrument had been bolted to a rocky outcrop in the hills of western Venezuela, quietly tracking the millimeter-scale movements of the Boconó fault, which was the likely source of the first of the two quakes. When Funvisis technicians went to recover the readings the sensor had stored, they found that the machine had gone missing. More than two months after the earthquakes, the organization still does not know who carried it off. The absent sensor is but one gauge of a state that has lost the capacity to govern. Venezuela once operated 250 to 300 seismic-monitoring stations; today, no more than five still function . Many of the engineers, physicians, nurses, firefighters, and rescue workers a country depends on when disaster strikes have long since left Venezuela—part of a generation-long exodus of skilled professionals from state institutions. President Trump has said that the oil-rich country will be run “properly” and “professionally,” but the earthquakes exposed Venezuela’s deficits. The highest expectations and fondest hopes—whether of Wall Street, Houston, or Caracas—will not conjure up the people needed to rebuild a country that has thoroughly hollowed out its professional classes. [ Read: The vicious cycle Trump may restart in Venezuela ] In just 20 years, Venezuela went from Latin America’s wealthiest nation to one of its poorest thanks to the mismanagement, corruption , and poor governance that began under the populist president Hugo Chávez, who served from 1999 to 2013, and continued under his successor, Nicolás Maduro. Interim President Delcy Rodríguez, who took over Venezuela after the United States captured Maduro in January, inherited a state that cannot marshall the technical expertise to rebuild what the quakes destroyed or to reconstruct an economy that collapsed long before the ground did. Rebuilding is a matter not merely of money and political will but of human capital. Bureaucrats, planners, regulators, and inspectors turn plans into functioning grids, ports, and clinics. Their absence may be the biggest obstacle facing American policy makers overseeing Venezuela’s reconstruction. V enezuela is not the first country to suffer brain drain to the point of institutional collapse. Afghanistan has reportedly struggled to stand up its health-care sector and civil service ever since many of its professionals fled the return of the Taliban in 2021. Haiti has been losing doctors, judges, and engineers for decades. But Venezuela’s case is one of particularly deliberate self-destruction, in a country where oil wealth helped produce a sizable middle class. Hostility toward the professional class was a hallmark of Chávez’s particular brand of socialism from the beginning. Adherents saw professional skills, when they were not explicitly placed in service of the revolution, as advancing the interests of capitalism and imperialism, the Venezuelan political scientist Guillermo T. Aveledo told me. In 2003, Guillermo García Ponce, a director at a pro-Chávez newspaper, went so far as to describe technocrats at state-owned companies as a “fifth column” to be “wiped out.” “For Chavismo, privilege always comes cloaked in a PowerPoint presentation,” the journalist Francisco Toro wrote in 2007. By dismissing expertise and deliberation as ideologically suspect, Toro added, “Chavismo is left to rely on the will of the leader alone.” The state’s public utilities were among the first institutions to confront the PowerPoint problem. Chávez replaced their professional managers with loyalists who were more compliant than competent, people who used to work in these companies told me. Jacqueline Faría, a Chavista engineer who took over the state-owned Caracas water company Hidrocapital in 1999, invested millions of dollars in a failed program to clean the Guaire River. Now she leads Rodríguez’s reconstruction efforts. In addition to Hidrocapital, the Chávez government proceeded to dismantle the corporate-style leadership of the Caracas metro and Venezuela’s largest electricity company, Edelca, and to place these companies under the control of military officers. It eventually did the same with Funvisis. In 2009, Chávez took direct control of the country’s airports and seaports. Water and power shortages , sometimes nationwide, became commonplace as mismanagement, corruption, and doctrinaire regulations gummed the works of nearly all of Venezuela’s public infrastructure. Consider Edelca’s two dam projects. The company began building the Caruachi dam in 1997, under Chávez’s predecessor, but finished it only after nine long years. It began building the Tocoma dam in 2007 and still has not finished it, despite almost $10 billion in investment. A Brazilian contractor involved in the work later admitted to paying Venezuelan officials and middlemen as much as $98 million in bribes from 2005 to 2016 to secure contracts. A U.S.-Argentine company will now take over the project. P erhaps no sector was more gravely affected by Chávez’s assault on professionalism than the oil industry. And no industry is more crucial to U.S. plans for Venezuela’s recovery—or more central to Washington’s interest in the country in the first place. Before Chávez, Venezuela’s oil company, known by its Spanish acronym PDVSA, was owned by the state but autonomously governed as a commercial entity. It set the gold standard for such an arrangement, expanding into international markets and fully acquiring Citgo, a major Houston-based refinery, in 1991. Much of the Venezuelan state ran on clientelism, but the oil company was meritocratic. Its research arm, the Venezuelan Institute of Oil Technology, or INTEVEP, employed about 170 full-time Ph.D. researchers and held roughly 1,200 American patents in the period before 2003, according to Francisco Monaldi, an energy expert. [ Jonathan Chait: Trump meant it literally when he said he was taking the oil ] That was the year Chávez began meddling in PDVSA’s affairs. He fired its board on live television and appointed a military officer to run the company. PDVSA’s workers went on strike in protest. Chávez fired more than 18,000 of them—dismissing, in one stroke, 60 to 80 percent of all provisioning, planning, maintenance, and exploration staff. The finance team was laid off almost entirely; state cronies took over an office that accounted for nearly all of Venezuela’s foreign-exchange earnings. INTEVEP’s scientists were replaced, Pánfilo Masciangioli, a researcher and manager at the institute from 1982 to 2010, told me, “with people who did not even know how important it was to publish a paper.” The institute’s patents fell to about 100 during the decade that followed. “The company’s gray matter was lost,” Monaldi told me. In its place came party loyalists and military men, who filled PDVSA’s vacancies and directed its revenues into Chávez’s populist schemes. Former employees scattered abroad. The number of Venezuelans in Alberta—the epicenter of Canada’s oil industry—rose from 465 in 2001 to 3,860 in 2011, and in Colombia, former PDVSA oil experts helped nearly double national oil production by 2011. Meanwhile, across the border, clientelism swelled PDVSA’s payroll from 28,841 in 2003 to 177,770 in 2014. The effect fully manifested a decade later: Global oil prices fell, and Venezuela’s ruined oil industry collapsed, its output falling from about 3 million barrels a day before Chavez’s PDVSA purge to an average of 512,000 a day in 2020. Employees of Venezuela’s state institutions came under continual pressure. In 2004, more than 2 million Venezuelans signed a referendum to recall Chávez. A lawmaker close to the president drew up what would become known as the “Tascón List” to identify and fire the petitioners from state institutions and companies. Hundreds lost their jobs. At the National Library, “a clique decided who was leaving and who was staying,” Mario Di Giacomo, an information specialist there for nearly 20 years, told me. “Dissent was not acceptable.” Loyalists replaced the professionals, and the library’s collections descended into neglect. Millions of archival records are decaying, Di Giacomo said. The Tascón List was but one way of identifying people for firing. At the Venezuelan Institute for Scientific Investigation, the country’s premier scientific-research center, the physicist Claudio Mendoza made a public comment mocking Venezuela’s nuclear ambitions in 2006 (he noted that the country would achieve little so long as it rejected scientific expertise). He was dismissed four days later. The Chavista zoologist Ángel Viloria took over the institute and systematically purged its scientists from 2006 to 2011. “You were either fired or forced to retire,” Mendoza told me. Venezuela slid from Latin America’s fifth-largest producer of scientific papers in the early 2000s to its 11th by 2022. By 2016, researchers who had emigrated accounted for roughly 33 percent of the country’s scientific publications; at least 68 percent of these scholars held doctoral degrees. T rump has promised that American investors will spend $100 billion to rebuild Venezuela’s “rotting” energy infrastructure, but he hasn’t said who will do the work. The simple truth is that Venezuela has rid itself of the technocrats who could deliver the recovery Washington has promised. Few will return to the bureaucracy that ejected them. Some have emigrated for good; among those who remain, many distrust the authoritarian government or do not wish to be associated with it. [ Read: The bizarre partnership between the U.S. and Venezuela ] The United States is currently overseeing talks between the Rodríguez government and the democratic opposition about the country’s recovery and reconciliation. It could use that platform to push for basing appointments to public institutions on relevant expertise rather than political loyalty and, in doing so, help restore confidence among the country’s professionals. Among the hollowed-out agencies that should be high on the list for rebuilding is Funvisis—not only for reasons of public safety but also because the geophysical data that Venezuela no longer collects are the raw material of modern oil exploration. Companies use seismic surveys to image a reservoir before they spend a dollar drilling into it, and Venezuela’s archives are dated, its instruments are scarce, and the geophysicists who once operated both are now working in Calgary or Houston or Bogotá. A state that cannot say whether the fault lines beneath it are moving is poorly placed to tell an investor what lies within the Orinoco Basin. Washington can disburse the oil money and lift the sanctions; it cannot staff the ministries. Only Venezuelans can do that. Ultimately, the country’s recovery will be measured less in barrels lifted or dollars banked than in how many of those professionals will go back to work for the state.

items.title: The Armored Sarcophagus Saving Ukrainian Soldiers
items.description: T he inside of an armored sarcophagus smells of gunpowder, gasoline, and gangrene. Remotely operated, unmanned ground vehicles, nicknamed MAULs, are revolutionizing casualty evacuations along the most dangerous sections of the Ukrainian front lines. They bristle with drone-jamming antennae and carry bulletproof black pods for carrying wounded soldiers to safety. The MAUL goes in when other options have failed. After every rescue, it is cleaned and disinfected. Vitaly, call sign “Ash,” is a medical-evacuation coordinator with the 1st Separate Medical Battalion. (He asked to be identified only by his first name and call sign for security reasons.) “You scrub and scrub,” he told me, “but the smell—it never goes away.” I asked Ash what MAUL stands for. “It’s not initials,” he explained. “It’s a Star Wars thing—you know, Darth Maul? We’ve got a few nerds here.” The name is in all caps because the battalion’s stencil kit has only capital letters. [ Read: Ukraine’s short-lived comeback ] On the battlefield, these new machines have become priority targets for Russia’s drone pilots. They know that, for the morale of the Ukrainian crews coordinating rescues, losing a comrade in vivid detail on the monitors tracking the mission can be devastating. Russian operators wait until the wounded are loaded, then strike. A erial drones have created a death zone on the front lines, up to 20 miles wide, where anything caught in the open is likely to be struck. Unmanned ground vehicles began arriving in late 2024, mostly running resupply routes parallel to the front. But a mission in early 2025 proved that they could do more than this—that they were capable of reaching deep into the death zone to remove personnel. That mission began with a Facebook post. In February 2025, near Kupiansk, Ukraine, a Russian advance trapped three Ukrainian soldiers from the 154th Mechanized Brigade behind enemy lines. All were wounded, two severely. For weeks, unit commanders attempted to pull them out. “We tried everything,” Kseniya Vynohradova, a veteran of the 154th who now leads an online support group for the unit, told me. Every effort failed. “The brigade dropped supplies by drone,” Vynohradova told me, “but there was no way to get the guys out.” After a month of fending off Russian attacks and surviving on air-dropped rations, the soldiers were ready to give up. Their wounds had turned gangrenous, and their chance of survival was near zero. “I did not know what else to do,” Vynohradova said, “so I turned to Facebook.” The first person to offer hope was Viktor Dolhopyatov. In a secret facility in central Ukraine, he runs Burevii, one of the country’s most innovative defense-tech companies. Russian bombardments have shattered most of the windows, but this superficial damage, common to thousands of buildings across the region, offers a kind of camouflage. From here, Burevii has transformed the modern battlefield. When Dolhopyatov read Vynohradova’s Facebook post, he answered immediately: “Tell us more, we want to help.” Burevii’s engineers were developing a ground drone at the time. It would need a few modifications for a mission deep into the death zone—anti-drone netting, software updates, and a trailer attachment to carry three soldiers at once—but it could be ready within days. Olha Garbovskaya had joined the company two weeks prior and threw herself into the mission. “We called our machine Ardal,” she told me, after a son of the Greek god of craftsmen and technology. With engineers still attaching its final pieces, Ardal was rushed to the front. The rescue began at dusk, with daylight fading but temperatures warm enough to partially mask Ardal’s heat signature. From a command bunker, Burevii’s engineers watched the mission unfold. High-definition screens displayed a ground’s-eye view from the drone. Overhead feeds tracked Ardal’s route to the stranded soldiers, who followed its progress over their radio. Without warning, a massive heat bloom filled the infrared monitors in the bunker. Ardal had struck a mine. “Our hearts sank,” Garbovskaya said. “The commanders told us we had less than a 1 percent chance of succeeding, and we feared they were right.” Over the radio, the stranded men responded stoically: “We can’t take any more—just finish us off.” They begged to be bombed by Ukrainian drones. The team from Burevii asked them to hold out a little longer. “Give us 48 hours,” Dolhopyatov said. “We have another machine.” The second Ardal followed a different path through the minefield, and overhead bomber drones scoured the route to clear suspected mines. Ardal finally reached the men’s trench. They emerged ragged and wounded, but alive. Overhead, Russian drones closed in. From the command bunker, medics offered encouragement over the radio: “Climb in fast—we’re getting you out.” Ardal carried them to safety, under the watchful eye of Ukrainian aerial drones. In the command bunker, Garbovskaya surveyed the scene. More than 50 people—pilots, medics, electronic warfare crews, engineers—had all assembled to save three men. F or most of history, recovering injured personnel from an active battlefield has not been a military priority. If the wounded could not make their way to safety, they were left until the fighting stopped. Serious injuries almost always ended in death, and the ratio of wounded to killed was about 3 to 1. During the First World War, evacuating wounded soldiers became its own professionalized combat discipline. Many injuries were still fatal, but the ratio of wounded to killed began to improve. By the time of the Vietnam War, the widespread adoption of helicopters and the doctrine of the “golden hour”—the narrow window in which medical intervention is most likely to save a life—drove the survival ratio to 5 wounded for every soldier killed. During America’s wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, rapid evacuation and advanced medical interventions brought survivability to historic highs. For every American soldier killed in those wars, approximately 10 survived their injuries. But in Ukraine, the death zone has made rapid evacuation all but impossible. Survivability has fallen, with a wounded-to-killed ratio of about 5 to 1. Units such as the 1st Medical Battalion are trying to change that. The old battlefield math held that in many instances, rescuing a wounded soldier required more resources and risk than could be justified for a single life. But Ukraine has opted for a different way of calculating. [ Read: Ukraine may be just the ally America needs ] The military has introduced a points system that assigns varying values to different missions, rewarding units with credits that can be traded for new gear and supplies. Under the “ePoints” scheme, a routine resupply run earns two to three points; a casualty evacuation earns upwards of 70. On today’s battlefield, saving a single Ukrainian soldier is worth more than destroying a Russian tank. I nside the death zone, Ukraine’s trenches are so difficult to reach that medics have had to reimagine the golden hour. Wound treatment must be provided on-site, by fellow soldiers. There simply are not enough medics for every trench. Andrii Fedoryshyn, call sign “Jared,” is a trainer with the 1st Med. “The best thing we can teach a soldier is combat first aid,” he told me. “It’s more important than knowing how to shoot.” The numbers bear this out. Less than 1 percent of the injuries seen by the 1st Med are gunshot wounds, and a soldier is far more likely to be called on to aid a buddy than to engage with the enemy. Everyone near the death zone, even journalists, carries a tourniquet. Many soldiers carry two or more, in the event that shrapnel severs multiple arteries. Once immediate care is provided, the waiting begins. “For a front-line soldier, evacuation can take weeks,” the deputy commander of the 1st Med, who asked to be identified by only his first name, Igor, told me. “We once evac’d a patient who had a tourniquet on for 33 days.” That soldier’s unit tried everything to get him out: six attempts, six failures, and multiple armored vehicles lost in the process. The decision was made to send in a MAUL. “He lost the limb,” Igor said. “But we saved his life.” As battlefield resources, MAULs are severely limited. Still, they are treated as expendable. Soldiers’ lives matter more. On average, two MAULs are lost for every five lives saved. I asked Ash, the battalion’s evacuation coordinator, if he ever got sentimental about the machines. “They’re tools,” he answered. “We don’t get attached.” The platoon commander, call sign “Devi,” interrupted. “Except for this one,” he said, pulling up a video on his phone. It showed a MAUL that had lasted 10 missions, surviving drones and mines and saving the lives of 11 soldiers. After it was finally destroyed, its operators compiled a tribute video and posted it online, endowing the dead MAUL with a small but devoted fan club. Officially, the logo of the 1st Med is a coiled snake, the ancient Greek symbol for medicine. The MAUL drivers have an unofficial logo of their own: a coffin overlaid with a progress indicator. They call themselves the “Tomb Raiders,” because, as Devi explained, “we bring people back from the dead.” Hence the movie posters plastered around the bunker, featuring Angelina Jolie in her Tomb Raider role. Opposite a wall of monitors, a scantily clad Jolie is covered in stickers featuring the coffin-and-timer logo. Each one represents a life saved. “When we fill the whole poster,” Igor explained, “we’ll auction it off to buy more machines.” As much as medics value their MAULs, the soldiers I spoke with hated them. “No windows, no ports,” one told me. “I would rather have less protection and see what’s coming at me.” Once sealed in, a patient’s only link to the outside is a single ray of light streaming through the hinge seam and an intercom connected to the medic. On a range far from the front, I rode inside a new MAUL undergoing testing. The coffin-like pod was stifling, and the bumpy ride nearly shook the bones out of my body. “I understand why soldiers hate it,” I told Devi. He received the feedback like a bad Yelp review. “Fair enough,” he said, “but a soldier able to complain is a soldier who survived.” The overwhelming majority of those rescued by a MAUL live to talk about it. In the command bunker, a casualty call came in: severe internal bleeding, with developing sepsis. A MAUL set off. Overhead surveillance drones tracked its progress as the bombers scanned the route for potential mines. Ash checked in via radio about the soldier’s condition. From the overhead feed, we saw the MAUL stop at a tree line. Two Ukrainian soldiers emerged from the foliage. One helped load the other into the sarcophagus, sealed the lid, and disappeared into the woods. Inside the command bunker, a calm professionalism prevailed. No voices were raised, except for Ash’s; he spoke loudly into his headset so that the patient could hear him over the noise of the machine. Midway through the eight-mile return journey, the electronic-warfare team detected a heavy Russian suicide drone, a Molniya, lurking overhead. The MAUL took cover, let the Molniya pass, then continued to the transfer point where a medical team awaited. As it approached the rendezvous, the Ukrainians spotted another approaching drone. “Three kilometers, closing,” came the call. The patient was quickly lifted into an armored vehicle, which sped off toward the field hospital. Ash’s job was done. He took off his headset and slumped into a couch. In the dim light, I noticed for the first time that he was wearing Crocs. His T-shirt, a Polish streetwear brand, said Ghosh . I sat next to him, somehow exhausted even though I had done nothing but observe. Through the walls I felt the thump of nearby drone strikes. No one else in the bunker seemed to notice them. I asked Ash what he did before the war. “Musical theater,” he said. “I was a performer.” I asked about his greatest fear as a combat medic. “Losing one of our guys en route,” he answered. Not seeing the gore of injuries, or wondering whether his bunker would be hit. His heaviest burden was the thought of a disabled MAUL, one of his patients trapped inside, unable to make it home. “Has this ever happened?” I asked. “Yes,” he said. “Twice.” In the Russian military, by contrast, being wounded and abandoned is the norm. At a POW camp in western Ukraine, I spoke with several Russian prisoners of war. “I was wounded in the legs,” one prisoner, who asked that I withhold his name for fear of reprisal, told me. “There was no rescue—my own guys left me to die.” The first medical attention he received was from the Ukrainian military. Reliable figures for Russia’s wounded-to-killed ratio are difficult to pin down, but conservative estimates place it at about 2 to 1, worse than the survival ratio of Russian soldiers during World War I. A t the foothills of Ukraine’s Carpathian Mountains , far from the front lines, lies a rehab facility for injured soldiers. I met Pavlo there, four months into his recovery from injuries sustained trying to rescue another soldier. He had successfully driven his truck to the pickup point for his wounded comrade when he was struck by a Russian drone. Shrapnel entered his abdomen, tore through his bladder, and broke his pelvis. Someone dragged him into a trench. Pavlo begged to stay there, remembering the wrecked and burning vehicles littering the road he drove in on. Over the radio, the medics insisted, “If you do not leave, you will die for sure.” [ Read: Ukraine planned to swarm Moscow airports with AI-guided drones ] At dusk, the unmanned ground vehicle came. Over the next three hours, the teams behind it—medics, ground-drone operators, bomber- and aerial-surveillance-drone pilots, and electronic-warfare crews—performed the intricate choreography needed to carry Pavlo to safety. From the top of a Carpathian ski resort, under a cloud-dappled sky, Pavlo recounted every detail, from his failed attempt to rescue his fellow soldier to the moment he went into surgery. Every few minutes, we glanced skyward to scan for threats. We were safe, but such habits die hard. Pavlo would soon return to his new wife, and he knew that this would have been impossible without the ground drone and the humans who operated it, all working together to save this one soldier. “I never met them,” Pavlo said. “A robot carried me, but people saved me. So many, just for me.” He looked up again. “I don’t even know their names.”

items.title: Cuba’s Old Economic Model Is ‘Exhausted’
items.description: I n September 2010 , an ailing Fidel Castro made a striking admission. The Atlantic ’s Jeffrey Goldberg had asked him whether the Cuban model was still worth exporting. “The Cuban model doesn’t even work for us anymore,” Castro bluntly told him . Sixteen years later, Carlos Fernández de Cossío, one of Cuba’s top diplomats, offered me a similar assessment of the state of the revolution, nearly seven decades on. In an interview in Washington, D.C., Cossío told me that Cuba’s Soviet-influenced system of central planning and state control “is exhausted.” The world, he said, has changed, and Cuba has to change with it. He stressed that Havana is open to pursuing that transformation in partnership with Washington. But coercive economic pressure, he argued, will make the task only more difficult. Coercive pressure is, in fact, the Trump administration’s strategy. Since President Trump returned to the White House last year, his administration has put an economic squeeze on Havana, including sanctions and fuel-shipment restrictions that have contributed to severe shortages and prolonged blackouts on the island. Trump’s approach to Cuba reflects a mix of ideological opposition, national-security concerns, and economic opportunism. Some within his administration object to Havana’s partnerships with U.S. adversaries, including Russia, China, and Iran. (Cossío claimed that Iran’s presence in Havana consisted of one Persian restaurant.) The administration has also cited Cuba’s failure to cooperate with U.S. law enforcement on migration concerns. This year, the two governments appeared open to working out some of these issues and acknowledged having direct contact. But Cuba’s foreign minister, Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla, told reporters in Havana earlier this month that neither negotiations nor an agenda for future talks has been established, despite Havana’s willingness to stay in touch. Since the U.S. military ousted Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in January, Trump has repeatedly warned that Cuba could be next. In May, CIA Director John Ratcliffe traveled to Havana to deliver Trump’s message that Washington was prepared to engage on economic and security issues, but only if Cuba made “fundamental changes.” Days later, the head of U.S. Southern Command met with Cuban military officials near Guantánamo Bay. A White House official, in a written response to my questions, conveyed Trump’s view that Cuba “has been horribly run for years” and said the United States is “ready to open a new chapter in the relationship.” The official added: “The only thing standing in the way of a better future are those who control Cuba for their own gain at the expense of the Cuban people.” Cossío and other top Cuban officials have sought to demonstrate that Cuba can change for the better on its own. But the gap between what Havana considers meaningful reform and what the Trump administration says needs to happen remains wide. Washington has demanded substantial changes, and although Havana is open to economic modernization, it insists that its political system is nonnegotiable. Prolonged blackouts have disrupted everyday life, and deteriorating water and sanitation systems have contributed to a surge in illnesses. Hospitals face fuel shortages and electricity disruptions, which affect refrigeration for medicines and vaccines. In eastern Cuba, UNICEF reported earlier this year, 481,000 people were relying on water trucks, and some families were being forced to use unsafe water because fuel shortages constrained pumping and other essential services. Against that backdrop, Cuba has been pursuing its own economic reforms. In June, the government approved 176 measures that expand private business, foreign investment, and private participation in banking, while giving investors a greater role in state-owned companies. The government also began allowing Cubans living abroad to own or invest in private businesses on the island. Subsequent measures have eased bureaucratic restrictions on private businesses and opened additional space for foreign investment, including in tourism. As Cossío and I discussed relations between Washington and Havana—which Cossío was careful to call “bilateral contacts,” not negotiations—he laid out what economic change in Cuba might look like. His country, he said, needs to move toward an economy “more dependent on financial instruments, on the market economy, with a much greater role for the private sector,” while leaving the state as a participant. He described the transformation now under way as the “most significant social and economic transformations” in Cuba in the past 60 years. T he U.S. is now applying extraordinary pressure on Cuba, to the point that Cuban officials have accused Washington of seeking to force political change. “They speak openly, openly about military aggression, and they are subjecting the people of Cuba to an unrelenting war,” Cossío told me. The deputy foreign minister made no demands for a new diplomatic initiative or a major U.S. aid package to alleviate Cuba’s distress. Trump, he said, has the power to put the relationship on the right path by removing restrictions on Americans traveling to the island. He could also restore Americans’ ability “to do business in Cuba, to trade with Cuba, to invest in Cuba if they wish.” “We’re not asking for a grant,” Cossío said. “We’re not asking for gifts or favors. We want the U.S. to stop punishing the Cuban economy” and its commercial relationships with countries around the world. This year, for example, Mexico’s state-owned oil company, Pemex, paused its oil exports to Cuba after the U.S. seized Maduro. And the Trump administration backed a lawsuit brought by a private U.S. docks owner against major cruise operators for using docks in Havana confiscated by Cuba’s government in 1960. The cruise companies maintain that their travel operations to Cuba were legal. [ Read: The schism within the Trump administration on Mexico ] The Trump administration says that its goal is not simply to open Cuba’s economy but also to pressure the Cuban government into making broader political change. Its policy calls for more freedom, democracy, human rights, and free enterprise in Cuba, while maintaining the U.S. economic embargo and restrictions on transactions that benefit the Cuban military and security apparatus. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the first person of Cuban descent to hold the position, has repeatedly portrayed the Cuban government as a threat to U.S. national security and argued that its ruling elite maintains control over the economy. This month, as Cuba was rolling out further measures to expand private investment, Rubio announced another round of sanctions against Cuban state-linked financial, mining, and energy entities, saying that the measures were aimed at those who sustain the regime. Cossío stressed that American companies could have a place in Cuba amid the changes if Washington eased its restrictions. “The U.S. could take advantage of that, become an important business partner in Cuba,” Cossío said. “They could invest. They could have a better relation with the emerging private sector in Cuba. They could benefit as a business opportunity.” Mindful that Trump is always seeking another win in relations with other nations, Cossío put it in terms the American president is likely to understand. “They could even claim a victory,” he said. I t’s hard to imagine Castro putting the proposition quite that way. Goldberg’s interview with Fidel Castro came as Fidel’s brother Raúl was beginning to loosen the state’s grip on the economy, allowing more small businesses to operate and opening limited avenues for foreign investment. Back then, Cuba was beginning to adopt some of the economic ideas that Washington had long demanded—even as U.S. policy prevented Americans from participating in the experiment. The new measures are a significant loosening of the economic system built around state control. But Cuba remains a one-party state. That may not sit well with the Trump administration, which says Cuba’s economic model cannot fundamentally change without altering its system of governance. Cuba’s critics in the U.S. point to the regime’s record of detaining political prisoners. The government this year announced it was releasing 2,010 prisoners, but Human Rights Watch, citing local advocacy groups, said in April that 700 or so political prisoners remained behind bars. Hundreds more faced house arrest and other restrictions. “The only thing worse than a Communist is an incompetent Communist. And so their system of government has to change because they will never be able to develop economically without those changes,” Rubio said in March. “Economic change is important. Giving people economic and political freedom is important, but they come hand in hand. They come together.” [ Read: How to break Cuba ] Cossío said that Cuba had been considering a transformation since at least 2011, but had hoped to undertake it under less punishing circumstances. After the opening made by the Obama administration, when the two countries restored diplomatic relations and the U.S. eased restrictions on travel and some commerce, Havana believed it might finally be able to move forward. The subsequent rollback of most President Obama–era policies in Trump’s first term, followed by more limited engagement under President Biden, changed that calculation. Now, Cossío said, Cuba has concluded that it cannot wait. “The country has changed. We’ve changed demographically. Our human resources have changed. The world has changed,” he told me. “We’ve come to the conclusion this year that, in spite of that, we cannot delay any more the transformation that we need to put in place in Cuba.” Sixteen years after Castro acknowledged that the Cuban model no longer worked, Havana is openly trying to evolve—and Cossío is telling Washington that it can either try to force the transformation from the outside or participate from within. But U.S. administrations, past and present, have long been skeptical that a system that has resisted changes for decades can meaningfully transform without radical changes at the top.

items.title: L’armée ukrainienne mène à Lyman sa deuxième contre-offensive majeure de l’année
items.description: Hier, mardi 15 septembre, le commandant du 3e corps d'armée ukrainien, Andriy Biletsky, a confirmé les rumeurs d'une contre-offensive en cours dans le nord de l'oblast de Donetsk. Biletsky a annoncé que les forces ukrainiennes avaient libéré l'équivalent de 85 km² de territoire autour de Lyman, et avaient contraint l'armée russe à replier ses approvisionnements en carburant vers l'oblast russe de Voronej, à une centaine de kilomètres Publication sur Telegram de Третій армійський корпус , 15 septembre 2026.'> 1 . Il s’agit de la première fois que Kiev repousse significativement l’armée russe dans ce secteur du front depuis près de quatre ans. Lyman, une ville du nord de l’oblast de Donetsk dont la population s’élevait à 20 000 habitants avant la guerre, avait été libérée en octobre 2022 par les forces ukrainiennes après cinq mois d’occupation russe. La situation s’était toutefois détériorée depuis : en novembre 2025, Deep State rapportait des infiltrations russes dans la ville depuis le sud-est. Le groupe notait alors que « la pression constante exercée par les forces russes et leur supériorité numérique peuvent à tout moment changer la situation ». L’opération, baptisée « Vivaldi », est entourée d’un silence opérationnel similaire à celui qui avait caractérisé la contre-offensive menée au premier semestre dans le sud du pays, et qui avait conduit à la libération de 745 km² de territoire dans les régions de Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk et Zaporijia. Ce « black-out médiatique » répond autant à des raisons de sécurité qu'à la volonté de ne pas inciter le commandement russe à allouer davantage de ressources pour repousser les avancées ukrainiennes. Les quatre années de guerre ont en effet montré que le décalage entre la perception de Moscou et la réalité des rapports de force sur le front avait tendance à créer des conditions favorables pour Kiev. En raison de la volonté des responsables militaires russes de ne pas communiquer au pouvoir politique les échecs ou l'absence de réussite sur le front, l'armée russe pourrait avoir laissé la situation se dégrader depuis plusieurs mois sans réagir à temps. Selon l’analyste Clément Molin, la contre-attaque ukrainienne dans le secteur de Lyman aurait été lancée dès la fin du mois de mai ВСУ отбросили российские войска под Лиманом в ходе операции « Вивальди », освобождены 75 км² », The Insider , 15 septembre 2026.'> 2 . Biletsky affirme que la libération de 85 km² ne constituerait que la première phase d’une opération plus longue, ce qui laisse supposer que le territoire libéré pourrait être plus important à l’issue de celle-ci. Fin août, Molin affirmait qu’environ 200 km² de terrain qui étaient sous contrôle russe « ont été perdus » Publication sur Telegram de Clément Molin , 30 août 2026.'> 3 . Selon l’ISW, les forces ukrainiennes auraient probablement déjà réalisé des avancées supérieures aux annonces de Biletsky Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, September 15, 2026 , Institute for the Study of War.'> 4 . Si ces gains restent inférieurs à ceux réalisés dans le sud du pays entre janvier et août, la reprise de l’initiative par Kiev dans ce secteur du front pourrait significativement retarder la progression russe dans la région de Donetsk. Selon des sources proches du Kremlin, Poutine voudrait avoir capturé la totalité de l’oblast au cours des six prochains mois. Fin août, Volodymyr Zelensky avait affirmé que le président russe avait fixé comme date butoir le 31 décembre 2026. Depuis 2022, Poutine a fixé 15 échéances à l'armée pour la capture de l'oblast de Donetsk – mais aucune n'a réussi à être respectée. L’article L’armée ukrainienne mène à Lyman sa deuxième contre-offensive majeure de l’année est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: An Electoral Mess in Missouri
items.description: B ethany Mann has put thousands of miles on her 2014 Toyota RAV4 while campaigning for office in Missouri’s Third Congressional District. The problem for Mann, her opponents, and the hundreds of thousands of voters who live there is that for months, no one has known precisely where the district’s boundaries are. Missouri jumped last year into the nation’s redistricting wars , pushing through a new congressional map backed by President Trump that would secure an additional Republican House seat in November. The plan has mostly collapsed, leading to a year of legal fights and confusion for voters. The partisan battle reached the Supreme Court last week and spurred a chaotic back-and-forth among the courts that changed the boundaries multiple times within a single hour. For now, the old map, which was adopted in 2022, is back in effect, but Republican candidates are still battling. A hearing in a federal appeals court is set for tomorrow—one day before the state is required to start making absentee ballots available to overseas voters. [ Read: The election deniers’ long game ] The mayhem in Missouri is the latest example of how uncertain and volatile the midterm elections have become. Republicans started the redistricting battles last year to gain partisan advantage during the midterms, and Democrats quickly followed. Missouri and nine other states have since redrawn their maps. On Monday, the Court blocked a Trump executive order that would have dramatically restricted voting by mail, a decision that Trump called a “big loss for Republicans, and America itself.” Voting-rights groups celebrated the decision, which they say prevents chaos. But with fewer than two months until Election Day, election-related litigation is still winding its way through the courts, and Trump continues to claim that the electoral system is rigged . “We’re talking about last-minute changes to election infrastructure, which could lead to either confusion or affect the outcome of the election,” Nate Persily, a Stanford University law professor, told me. “And it is a serious problem, particularly in our current context when voter confidence in the election infrastructure has collapsed.” M issouri’s saga began shortly after the state legislature passed the new, GOP-friendly map at the urging of the White House last September. Opponents seized on a quirk in the state constitution that empowers citizens to petition for a referendum on an act of the state legislature. In December, an advocacy group submitted more than 305,000 signatures asking for a vote before the new map would be put into effect—which would leave the old map in use for the election this fall. Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, a Republican, had until August 4, the state’s primary date, to certify the referendum for November’s ballot. For months, it’s been unclear which map would actually be used. Democratic candidates, including Mann, told me that they’d stumped through both the new and old versions of their district—a choice that took extra manpower, organizing, and money. Others, including Representative Bob Onder, a Republican whom Mann is challenging, told me that they’d campaigned off of the revised 2025 map. [ Quinta Jurecic: Rules designed to create chaos ] “We knew that they were going to be enacting this gerrymandered scheme,” Mann said. “So our strategy, not just in the Third Congressional but as a Democratic Party as a whole, was to beat these congresspeople on any map that they offer.” But the morning of the primary came, and Hoskins had still not certified the referendum. He directed election administrators to hold the primary under the 2025 map. At 4 p.m. that day, an hour before the referendum deadline, Hoskins rejected the petition on state constitutional grounds. Candidates won their primaries based on the gerrymandered map. A month later, the situation got even more complex. On September 3, the Missouri Supreme Court unanimously ruled against Hoskins, finding that the referendum petition was legal and should not have been rejected. It ordered the 2022 map to be used in November. Hoskins appealed the decision to the U.S. Supreme Court, which rejected his arguments last Tuesday. Thirty minutes later, a federal district judge ruling on a separate lawsuit ordered that the 2025 map must be used in November. Citing that decision, Hoskins announced that Missouri would use the new gerrymandered map—leading the Missouri Supreme Court to threaten him with contempt of court. The U.S. Supreme Court quickly chimed in again and restored the old map, for now; Hoskins was briefly held in contempt for continuing to insist that the 2025 map was valid, but he quickly switched his position to match that of the U.S. Supreme Court. Legal experts told me that it is highly unlikely that the appeals court would change the map again, but as the past two weeks have shown, nothing is certain. Both sides agree that the situation is a mess. Republicans I spoke with blamed the Missouri Supreme Court for rejecting the 2025 map after it had already been used for a primary. Democrats—and the majority of legal experts I spoke with—blamed Hoskins for waiting until the last available hour to reject the petition, a move that effectively forced the primary to be conducted with the 2025 map, which his party drew up. They said that the arguments should have played out in court months ago. Hoskins disagreed. “I take my job and oath of office very seriously,” Hoskins told me. “I met that deadline, my constitutional deadline, of August 4. I would say those that don’t like that deadline and want to see that deadline change, they need to contact their lawmaker . ” Some of the federal officials whose seats are on the line are, like voters, trying to figure out what’s going on and who is to blame. Onder, who is suing to reinstate the new map, told me that he and voters “operated on the assumption” that the 2025 map was the correct one. “To the extent this has been thrown into confusion and chaos, the fault is entirely [on] the part of the Missouri Supreme Court.” Representative Emanuel Cleaver, whose seat was supposed to be wiped out by the new map, told me that he had been campaigning “all over the state” over the past few weeks because of his uncertainty about which district he’d be in. “There’s been a fog over the state of Missouri,” Cleaver said. “We are now spending time trying to erase the confusion.” [ Read: The election system wasn’t built for this ] The bulk of the work is now in the hands of local election administrators, who are scrambling to prepare for the midterms on a condensed timeframe and with a confused electorate. Kurt Bahr, a Republican and the St. Charles County elections director, told me that he’s printing ballots under the old 2022 map but is preparing contingency plans in case courts once again change which map to use. In Boone County, where about 40 percent of voters would shift into a new district under the 2025 map, the clerk Brianna Lennon has provided a lookup tool so voters can see their districts under both maps. She said that she and her staff have been working to inform voters about what’s happening without causing needless panic. “These things are always being argued over and fought over by people who don’t have to run the election,” Eric Fey, the Democratic director of elections in St. Louis County, told me. Election administrators, he said, are the “folks that are left holding the bag at the end of the day.” Last year, Onder posted a clip of a speech in which he recounted speaking with Trump about redistricting. “I said, ‘Mr. President, do you want us to draw you an extra congressional seat in Missouri?,’” Onder said, adding that the state, which voted for Trump by 18 points and has Republican supermajorities in the state legislature, was poised under the old map to send “two progressive Democrats” to Congress. Missouri’s 2025 map aims to net an additional Republican seat in the House by carving Kansas City—long represented by Cleaver—into three districts that extend into rural central Missouri and strongly favor Republicans. The fate of Independence Boulevard Christian Church, in northeast Kansas City, exemplifies this gerrymandering tactic, known as “cracking.” Under the 2025 map, the church is in one district, the parking lot in another, and a market across the street in a third. “Before, there already were people who were saying [voting] doesn’t matter; they had already felt disenfranchised,” Mindy Fugarino, the pastor of the church, told me. “I think there are some folks just using this as another reason to disengage.” The “downward spiral” of extreme partisan gerrymandering over the past year risks disillusioning people, Richard Pildes, a constitutional-law professor at New York University, told me. “It leads to many voters feeling the system is being manipulated, that the system’s rigged,” he said. [ Read: Out of the gerrymandering darkness, a new hope for reform ] Both Democrats and Republicans in Missouri told me they feel cheated as the map continues to change. St. Charles County Republican Central Committee Chair Bob Eno told me he believes that the state supreme-court ruling took away people’s chances to choose their own representation by shifting the state back to the old map after primary votes had already been cast. Pat Harcourt, who lives in Wright City, initially thought that her Democratic ballot was incorrect for the August primary. But it wasn’t—her address had moved into a different district under the gerrymandered map. “And here I am writing postcards to people, ‘Your vote counts,’” Harcourt told me. “Well, I don’t know. Maybe it counts, but it may not be in your congressional district.” Mitchell Clem, a Republican voter whose district also moved under the new map, told me that he doesn’t like gerrymandering but understands that Missouri is part of a national trend. “We need to fix this,” Clem, who lives in the St. Louis suburb of O’Fallon, said. “It’s just gotten out of hand.” The drawing of congressional districts has always seemed subjective, and the rules for drawing them have been scrutinized since gerrymandering was first deployed as a political tactic more than 200 years ago. But as partisanship continues to deepen, the rules keep shifting far too late in the process, and voters try, perhaps in vain, just to keep up.

items.description: (Ouagadougou, 15 septembre 2026). Le Ministre Secrétaire général de la Présidence du Faso, Pr Zakaria SORÉ, Coordonnateur national de l'Initiative présidentielle pour une Éducation de Qualité pour tous (IPEQ), a donné, ce mardi matin à Ouagadougou, le coup d'envoi officiel des épreuves du concours de détection des talents scientifiques féminins, dénommé « HAKILI Mousso ». Il était accompagné à l'occasion de la Ministre Conseillère spéciale du Président du Faso, chargée du développement technologique, Dr Floriane OUÉDRAOGO/ZONGO. Après une semaine d'immersion et de préparation en internat au Lycée scientifique national de Ouagadougou, les 84 candidates sélectionnées à l'échelle nationale ont entamé les épreuves écrites. Titulaires d'un baccalauréat scientifique de la session 2026, ces jeunes filles se mesurent entre elles à travers différentes épreuves et sous-matières en mathématiques, physique et chimie.

items.title: The American Age Is Over
items.description: The American age that followed World War II was bound to end eventually. What’s shocking is how suddenly that moment has arrived. In the past six months, America’s power—long exemplified by the world’s best warfighting equipment and most highly trained military personnel, a global network of bases and logistics systems, and military and diplomatic partnerships with all corners of the world—has proved insufficient to defeat Iran, a repressive, economically stagnant regime armed with cheap missiles and drones. For years, virtually everyone thought that, in a crisis, Washington could draw on deeper reserves of money, troops, munitions, and diplomatic support than any other nation. Even when U.S. forces faced setbacks in conflicts such as Vietnam, Iraq, and Afghanistan, a widespread assumption about America’s fundamental strength reassured allies and deterred foes. Yet that assumption also promoted a complacency that has left the U.S. military exposed now that even inexpensive, mass-produced weaponry can be guided with deadly accuracy. President Trump did not erode U.S. capabilities on his own. But Trump’s war with Iran has revealed just how the underlying dynamics of global power have shifted—and just how much American might has decayed. Since Britain’s postwar retreat from the Middle East, the United States has been the most important military power in that volatile region. In 1980, the Carter administration asserted that America would guarantee the free flow of oil and other commodities out of the Persian Gulf to the wider world. The success of the Carter doctrine required hostile governments, which then included the Soviet Union as well as the new theocracy in Iran, to believe that the United States could and would take decisive military action against anyone who dared to close the Strait of Hormuz, through which much of the world’s petroleum, and other vital commodities, has long passed. [ Read: Iran unleashed ] Until recently, the array of American bases surrounding Iran gave that country’s leaders every reason to fear being overwhelmed militarily if they moved to control the strait. Yet the regime remains intact, even after attacks by the United States and Israel succeeded in killing top Iranian leaders, and its long-range missile and drone attacks managed to elude American air defenses and incapacitated many U.S. facilities. In March, fewer than two weeks into the fighting, The New York Times identified 17 American bases, air-defense installations, and diplomatic facilities that had been hit. Among them were some of the U.S. military’s important staging points: the Fifth Fleet’s headquarters in Bahrain as well as the Ali Al Salem Air Base, Camp Arifjan, and Camp Buehring in Kuwait. The effect of these losses on U.S. operations was nearly instantaneous. A key reason the Trump administration did not militarily escalate with Iran over the summer, despite all of its threats to do so, was the loss of the base in Bahrain—which the Navy relied on for decades to resupply ships in the Middle East. Instead, the so-called logistical tail for U.S. naval operations had to stretch all the way to Diego Garcia , a British-controlled island in the Indian Ocean more than 2,000 miles from the Strait of Hormuz. Complications to resupply efforts raise costs, reduce operational efficiency, and add to the strain on military personnel. Disrupted logistics contributed to the long deployment of the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln, which led in turn to low morale. According to Stars and Stripes , families of crew members on the Lincoln feared that the many months at sea were causing serious mental-health problems. For the moment—and likely for longer—the bases taken out of commission by Iranian attacks have been largely abandoned as operational facilities because of the continuing threat to U.S. personnel and equipment. At a recent town-hall meeting, Navy Times has reported , a service member asked Admiral Daryl Caudle about retrieving personal items from the Bahrain base. “We’re not getting back in there anytime soon,” Caudle responded. “I just want to be completely honest with that.” The vulnerability of U.S facilities near Iran is so great and the prospective cost of repair is so large that, as The Washington Post reported last month , administration officials might not want to rebuild them at all. One way to spin the situation is as a “once-in-a-generation chance for the Pentagon to reconsider its presence” in the Persian Gulf region, as the Post put it. But the basic fact is that defending key facilities against even a less technologically advanced foe such as Iran is not something that the U.S. military can currently do. The diminution of U.S. strength has a cascading effect. To maintain its military effort against Iran, the United States has had to strip the western Pacific of vital equipment. The Trump administration finally relieved the Abraham Lincoln last month; taking its place in the Arabian Sea was the USS George Washington, which is normally based in Japan. Its normal task is to discourage military action by China—a deterrence that is now greatly weakened. This desperate move only underscores that American military resources, however enormous relative to most other countries’, are not infinite. The war with Iran has depleted stockpiles of some of the Pentagon’s most important and advanced weaponry. By the end of April, cautious studies were estimating that the United States had already run dangerously low in THAAD (terminal high altitude area defense) munitions, Patriot interceptors, and Tomahawk cruise missiles. Shortages have worsened since then. For years, the United States has focused on building so-called exquisite systems—advanced weaponry that is produced in limited quantities at a high per-unit cost. This approach was in part an adaptation to the post-9/11 War on Terror, in which U.S. forces focused on counterinsurgency and fought enemies that lacked the capacity to mount and sustain serious attacks on American logistics. Under those circumstances, the Pentagon built up a broad array of munitions but not deep stockpiles of them. At current production rates, the United States will need several years to build supplies back to where they were when Trump went to war in February—and even those levels in hindsight look far too weak to maintain America’s long-standing global position amid a shift toward mass-produced precision-guided drones. The erosion of American manufacturing superiority is an old story, but it is a key element for understanding the end of the American age. The U.S. could once outbuild other powers by tapping into civilian production. During World War II, Americans retooled the automotive industry to build aircraft. Today, relative to the rest of the world, the United States does almost no civilian shipbuilding. China, in comparison, makes about 50 percent of the ships in the world and controls about 80 percent of the world’s drone manufacture. Having built its military to prevail in a burst of high-intensity fighting, the United States simply lacks the equipment, stockpiles, and rested forces to engage China for any extended period of time. In the past, the United States could rely on allies to amplify its own power. Nations that shared values or at least interests with Washington have hosted bases, provided diplomatic support for American initiatives, shared intelligence, and sent troops and equipment to support American-led military operations. Today, traditional allies have capabilities that the U.S. sorely needs. For example, Japan and South Korea are the second- and third-largest shipbuilding powers in the world. Rather than recognizing that it needs allies more than ever, the current U.S administration perceives governments that have followed American leadership for decades as free riders, annoyances, even hindrances. Recently, President Trump has been critical of South Korea and praised his supposedly great relationship with North Korea’s dictator, Kim Jong Un. Never mind that South Korea and North Korea are still technically in a state of war, and North Korea has nuclear weapons that could devastate its neighbor to the south and potentially other U.S. allies farther afield. Meanwhile in Europe, the U.S. government has distanced itself from long-standing democracies and moved closer to the Russian dictatorship of Vladimir Putin. Since returning to the White House, Trump has scaled back the American provision of security to Europe. Earlier this year, the Pentagon announced plans to withdraw 5,000 troops from Germany, and the administration has launched a defense-posture review that heralds further cuts. The U.S. is making no secret of its goal of turning over more and more of the responsibility of defending Europe to the Europeans. Leaders in Europe are taking these moves seriously and are making plans to rely less on the United States. Germany is considering whether to help the U.K. modernize its nuclear weapons so that Europe has a nuclear deterrent if the United States pulls out. [ Read: Europe without America ] The United States has even begun to alienate Canada. Trump has regularly talked about his desire to incorporate Canada as the 51st state. He has also launched a trade war that, by his own account, will be “devastating” to the Canadian economy. Americans have now twice elected a president who overtly seeks to reframe traditional alliances as zero-sum relationships in which the United States needs to do less and its former partners more. Leaders and voters in those countries might reasonably conclude that Americans do not know or do not care what they are giving up. Americans have long benefited from peaceful integration with Canada. The U.S. could go to war with Iran in part because of its large base network in Europe. The disruption of long-standing alliances will be devastating to America’s global position. Other countries are already adjusting to newly revealed American weaknesses. Pakistan, Turkey, and Saudi Arabia—all long-term U.S. partners—recently signed their own defense pact. Now that Iran is exercising control over the Strait of Hormuz, Oman, on the waterway’s opposite shore, is inching toward closer cooperation with Tehran. Other Gulf States are reaching out to Iran as well. Even Saudi Arabia, which for decades based its security on massive purchases of U.S. weapons and the hosting of U.S. forces, must reassess its choices after Trump told its de facto ruler that the U.S. will not assist the country in its war with the Houthis. Meanwhile, South Korea is improving relations with China, and European states are thinking more and more of a European-wide defense association. These are all strong signs that the countries around the world are losing confidence in America’s capabilities—and its intent. Unfortunately for the United States, the administration seems more intent on hiding problems than correcting them. The Defense Department has forced out key staffers at Stars and Stripes and demanded, in an investigation of leaks about munitions shortages and other matters, that certain Pentagon employees take polygraph tests . Even if the United States tries to revert to more of its earlier way of doing business, recent events suggest that its global reach will decrease. How the rest of the world will adapt to that change is hard to say. The American age may not give way to dominance by China, because that country has problems of its own and other states in Asia, such as India, are growing to balance it. Democratic nations that look after their own defense more diligently, rather than relying on American protection, might conceivably benefit. The world might also be in store for a very chaotic period of wars and competitions. All of history’s previous superpowers have eventually declined. The emergence of East Asia as the center of the world’s economic output was always going to reduce American influence. The transition from one global age to the next is seldom evident in the moment. When Russia invaded Ukraine four and a half years ago, the potential of mass-produced drones had not yet become clear. As recently as February, few experts would have predicted that the United States—a global colossus for more than 80 years—would end up so hamstrung by Iran. But the conflict reveals something important: The American age has come to an end. U.S. global dominance cannot continue without the power sources that brought it about.

items.title: Burkina Faso : Le commandant Ismaël Sombié salue l’engagement des investisseurs privés dans l’agriculture dans le Nakambé
items.description: Dans le cadre du suivi de la campagne agropastorale 2026-2027, le ministre d'État chargé de l’Agriculture, le commandant Ismaël Sombié, a effectué une visite des sites agricoles de la région du Nakambé, le 15 septembre 2026. En premier lieu, le ministre a visité une exploitation agricole de 72 hectares dans la commune de Bagré. Dans ce champ exploité par Bagré pôle, il y est cultivé uniquement du maïs. C'est une nouvelle stratégie qui repose sur un modèle d'agriculture plus performant, structuré et avec un grand rendement. Cette stratégie est aussi appliquée pour les autres spéculations comme le riz et le niébé. La délégation du ministère a aussi pris des nouvelles des exploitations agricoles des entrepreneurs privés. Conformément à l'appel du Président du Faso en 2025, ces derniers se sont investis dans la production agropastorale. Le premier site visité est exploité par le groupe Coris. L'entreprise a emblavé 114 hectares. Elle a fait pousser du maïs sur 82 hectares et le reste de la superficie a été consacré au sésame et au soja. Quant au deuxième exploitant, il a emblavé une superficie de 71 hectares. C'est possible de créer de la richesse en produisant, c'est possible de créer de la richesse en élevant, commandant Somnié©️Faso7 Le commandant Ismaël Sombié a traduit sa satisfaction aux agro-investisseurs pour avoir adhéré à l'initiative. Il a rappelé que l'agriculture est un secteur générateur de richesses et d’emplois. Pour lui, le secteur privé, notamment les transformateurs, gagnerait plus à s'intéresser à la production. Il a annoncé que le ministère, à travers la société Faso Agropole (SOFA), est en phase d'aménager 2 194 hectares au profit des agro-investisseurs. « C'est possible de créer de la richesse en produisant, c'est possible de créer de la richesse en élevant, c'est possible de créer de la richesse en transformant. Nous les (NDLR, les agro-investisseurs) attendons. Nous créons les conditions pour que leurs investissements puissent être viables, rentables et durables (…). Nous souhaitons que les acteurs du privé puissent non pas seulement se contenter de transformer, mais également de produire », a-t-il souligné. Des exploitations agricoles des entrepreneurs privés©️Faso7 Les entrepreneurs ont souligné avoir reçu un accompagnement du ministère à travers ses services techniques pour emblaver les sites. En dépit du caractère de la saison pluvieuse, les techniciens ont assuré que les semis présentent une bonne physionomie et que la campagne agricole se déroule bien dans la région. « Ce sont des échantillons que nous avons voulu montrer pour que vous ayez une perception de la réalité de la campagne telle que ça se passe au niveau de l'Agro-pôle du Nakambé. Et ça se déroule très bien et nous escomptons donc de très bonnes productions. Les champs que vous avez pu observer, si vous regardez la qualité des épis vous-mêmes, vous pouvez estimer le rendement. Au minimum, nous serons autour de 5 tonnes par hectare sur ces différents sites que vous avez effectivement vus », a expliqué Oula Ouattara, directeur général de la société Faso Agropole. Une partie du périmètre fourrager de Zangoula©️Faso7 La visite s'est poursuivie sur le périmètre fourrager de Zangoula. Il est de 18,5 hectares et les producteurs ont emblavé 10 ha de maralfalfa, 4 hectares de niébé, 2,5 hectares de brachiaria et 1,5 hectare de dolique. Pour une phase d'essai, Oula Ouattara, a noté que les espèces présentent une bonne physionomie. Il a ajouté qu'en perspective, ces sites seront transformés progressivement en prairies. « L'objectif est double : répondre aux ambitions d'approvisionner nos abattoirs que nous sommes en train de construire, que vous avez vus au niveau de Fada, répondre aux ambitions d'approvisionner nos unités de production laitière avec Faso Kossam, et répondre aux ambitions de faire rentrer notre cheptel et de consolider notre économie », a-t-il ajouté. Le directeur de la SOFA a invité les acteurs à être sereins, car la campagne présente une tendance normale. Selon les prévisions de la météo, dit-il, les pluies devraient se poursuivre jusqu'au mois d'octobre afin de permettre aux agriculteurs de parfaire leurs récoltes. Cheick Habib Désiré BAYILI Faso7 L’article Burkina Faso : Le commandant Ismaël Sombié salue l’engagement des investisseurs privés dans l’agriculture dans le Nakambé est apparu en premier sur Faso7 .

items.title: La BNG inaugure une nouvelle agence à Soumbouya et renforce sa présence à Boffa
items.description: Dans le cadre de sa politique de proximité et de son engagement en faveur d’une meilleure accessibilité aux services bancaires, la Banque Nationale de Guinée (BNG) poursuit l’extension de son réseau à l’intérieur du pays. La banque a inauguré ce samedi 12 septembre 2026, une nouvelle agence à Soumbouya, dans la commune rurale de Tamita, préfecture de Boffa. La cérémonie d’inauguration a réuni les autorités administratives, communales, coutumières et religieuses, ainsi qu’une forte mobilisation des populations de Soumbouya et des localités environnantes. Dans une ambiance festive et conviviale, les habitants ont répondu massivement à ce rendez-vous marquant l’arrivée d’un nouveau service bancaire au cœur de leur communauté. La cérémonie a débuté par des bénédictions et des prières conduites par l’imam de la mosquée de Soumbouya, avant de laisser place aux différentes allocutions. Prenant la parole au nom de la BNG, le Directeur général adjoint, M. Mohamed Lamine Thierno Camara, a d’abord salué la présence des autorités et des populations avant de revenir sur l’histoire et l’évolution de la banque. Il a notamment souligné l’importance stratégique de cette nouvelle implantation pour la BNG et pour les populations locales. « Cette nouvelle agence représente ainsi bien plus qu’un point de présence supplémentaire pour la BNG. Elle constitue un espace de rencontre, de conseils et de collaboration avec l’ensemble des acteurs qui contribuent au développement de Boffa. » Pour son intervention, M. Ansou Conté, Directeur commercial de la BNG, a pour sa part insistée sur l’importance de construire une relation durable avec la clientèle. « Bâtir une relation durable avec notre clientèle, fondée sur la confiance, l’écoute et la qualité de service. » Cette vision traduit l’ambition de la banque de placer la proximité et la qualité de l’expérience client au cœur de son développement. À travers cette implantation, la BNG entend ainsi renforcer la proximité avec sa clientèle, faciliter l’accès aux services financiers et mieux accompagner les acteurs économiques de la préfecture de Boffa et des localités environnantes. L’ouverture de cette agence a également été favorablement accueillie par les autorités locales. Dans son intervention, le maire de la commune de Boffa, M. Tafsir Soumah, a salué l’initiative de la BNG et exprimé le souhait de voir la banque poursuivre son expansion dans la préfecture. S’adressant directement au Directeur général adjoint de la BNG, il a plaidé pour davantage de proximité avec les populations : « Nous vous prions de multiplier les agences à Boffa. » Ce plaidoyer traduit l’importance accordée par les autorités locales au développement de l’offre de services financiers et au renforcement de l’inclusion financière dans la région. La nouvelle agence devrait également répondre aux besoins des entreprises et des travailleurs présents dans la zone. Alseny Camara, représentant de la société SD Mining, partenaire de cette initiative, s’est réjoui de l’ouverture de l’agence. Il a notamment mis en avant les opportunités qu’elle représente pour les nombreux employés de son entreprise qui ne disposent pas encore d’une relation bancaire. Selon lui, la présence de la BNG à Soumbouya permettra de combler une partie de ce déficit et de faciliter l’accès des travailleurs aux services bancaires de proximité. L’ouverture de cette agence apparaît ainsi comme une réponse concrète aux besoins croissants des populations, des entreprises et des acteurs économiques locaux. Au-delà de sa dimension institutionnelle, l’événement a également été placé sous le signe de la culture locale. La troupe préfectorale de Boffa a offert aux invités une prestation artistique mêlant chants, danses et expressions traditionnelles. Une séquence particulièrement appréciée du public, qui a permis de mettre à l’honneur la richesse culturelle et le patrimoine de la localité. Le moment fort de la cérémonie est intervenu avec la coupure officielle du ruban inaugural. Le Représentant du préfet de Boffa, l’autorité présente a officiellement déclaré ouverte la nouvelle agence de la BNG à Soumbouya, dans la commune rurale de Tamita, préfecture de Boffa. La coupure du ruban, effectuée en présence des autorités locales et du Directeur général adjoint de la BNG, a ainsi marqué le lancement officiel des activités de cette nouvelle agence. À travers l’ouverture de cette nouvelle agence, la BNG réaffirme ainsi sa volonté de renforcer progressivement son maillage territorial et de contribuer à une plus grande inclusion financière en Guinée. La cérémonie s’est achevée par une photo de famille réunissant les autorités, les représentants de la BNG, les partenaires, les invités et les populations. Un cocktail convivial a ensuite permis aux différents participants de poursuivre les échanges dans une atmosphère chaleureuse. Les festivités se sont prolongées dans les rues avec une parade de motards à travers la ville, accompagnée d’une opération de distribution de flyers auprès des populations, donnant une dimension davantage populaire et promotionnelle à l’événement. Avec l’ouverture de cette nouvelle agence à Soumbouya, la BNG franchit une nouvelle étape dans sa stratégie de proximité et d’inclusion financière. Pour les populations de Soumbouya, de Tamita et des localités environnantes, cette implantation constitue une nouvelle opportunité d’accéder plus facilement aux services bancaires et de participer davantage à la dynamique économique locale. À Soumbouya, une nouvelle page s’ouvre donc pour la BNG, avec une ambition claire : être toujours plus proche de ses clients et s’inscrire durablement au cœur du développement des communautés.

Y lo mismo me pasa con Lamine Yamal, a este con más razón porque defiende los colores de mi equipo y consiguió algo inédito a los ojos de los dioses y los hombres: que mi padre se comprase una camiseta de la selección española y la luciera orgulloso durante todo el verano mientras cuidaba los tomates de su huerta. Como harían bien ustedes en reclamar explicaciones sobre el significado de la palabra laxe (en gallego, una piedra más o menos grande, más o menos plana, más o menos lisa, que sobresale del terreno, pero tampoco mucho; a veces ni siquiera sobresale). items.title: Maresca defends VAR officials after Man City benefit from error
items.description: Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca on Wednesday expressed sympathy for VAR officials after his team benefited from a clear error in their 1-0 win against Manchester United. Erling Haaland scored a controversial winner in the 60th minute at Old Trafford on Sunday to make it four wins out of four for City in the Premier League. Haaland was initially flagged offside but VAR ruled he was being played onside by United defender Patrick Dorgu, neglecting to take account of the position of Enzo Fernandez, who was clearly offside and was interfering with play. Refereeing body Pro Ref acknowledged an “error of judgment”, saying that the video assistant referee should have recommended an on-field review. But Maresca spoke up for the officials ahead of Thursday’s League Cup third round match against Championship side Norwich. “Sometimes they go for you, the decisions, sometimes they go against you,” he said. “But also it’s not easy, I think, for the VAR, for the people that are in front of the screen, and in 10 seconds, 20 seconds they have to make a decision. “It’s not easy for them. Sometimes they make some mistakes. I make mistakes, players make mistakes, I think it’s part of our job.” Maresca said he was unhappy with the intense focus on the offside goal following an impressive win for his team, who were reduced to 10 men when Phil Foden was sent off in the first half. The Italian, who replaced Pep Guardiola as manager in June, reminded reporters of a controversial incident when he was Guardiola’s assistant in the 2022/23 season. Bruno Fernandes’s goal was given despite the presence of Marcus Rashford in an offside position in a 2-1 win for United at Old Trafford. Maresca said he was still waiting for officials to say sorry. “Three years ago, when I was here, it happened exactly the same against Man United,” said the former Chelsea boss. “We lost the derby there. The goal was not a regular goal, if you remember. To be honest, no one apologised. We are still waiting for the apology for that goal. “Sometimes it happens for you, sometimes it happens against you. It’s football.” Maresca brushed aside a question on whether he was pleased there would be no VAR in place in the early rounds of the League Cup, bringing the focus back to Sunday’s win. “I’m pleased with the unbelievable performance from the players on Sunday,” he said. “I’m very pleased with that. Talking about one moment after that game, when we played for 70-75 minutes with 10 players, I think it’s quite poor. I think the performance was unbelievable.” The post Maresca defends VAR officials after Man City benefit from error appeared first on Vanguard News .
